content: 1. Assessment of VMMC Uptake in Mozambique: The progress in voluntary medical male circumcision (VMMC) uptake among adult men was evaluated using several methods. These included creating detailed tables to track VMMC coverage across provinces, broken down by age groups, and generating figures that overlaid VMMC coverage with unmet needs among men aged 10–29 years. Additionally, data from the Site Capacity and Productivity Assessment Tool highlighted the utilization rates of VMMC sites in Tete Province, Mozambique. By April 2018, data from the DMPPT 2 model provided a detailed breakdown of VMMC coverage by province and age group, visualized through a heat map. Provinces with less than 50% coverage were marked in red, 50–70% in yellow, and over 70% in green. 2. Lessons Learned in Mozambique: Visualizing data on unmet needs, epidemiological impact, and service delivery capacity through maps and graphics helped program planners focus on areas with the greatest need and potential impact. Combining demographic modeling (accounting for aging, mortality, and birth rates) with program data allowed for the development of metrics to assess changes in VMMC uptake by age group. 3. Case Study in KwaZulu-Natal, South Africa: KwaZulu-Natal (KZN) has the highest HIV prevalence in South Africa but historically low VMMC uptake due to the banning of traditional male circumcision by Zulu King Shaka in the 19th century. The practice was reinstated in 2009 by the reigning king. Despite achieving 1 million circumcisions in nine years, half of the eligible population remains uncircumcised. Barriers included lack of awareness about VMMC benefits, low perceived relevance, and anticipated stigma for men grouped with younger boys at service points. Initiatives included endorsements by traditional leaders, with the king and his son actively promoting VMMC. The USAID VMMC Project provided services in diverse settings, including public health facilities, private practices, and VMMC camps. Mobilization strategies targeted men in workplaces, informal settlements, and social spaces. 4. Case Study in Tanzania: In Tanzania, older men faced barriers to accessing VMMC services, such as distance, waiting times, and lack of privacy. The Jhpiego-led AIDSFree project collaborated with the Sauti project to integrate VMMC with community-based HIV testing services (HTS). Mobile teams provided same-day VMMC services alongside HTS, targeting uncircumcised men identified through data reviews. This approach increased VMMC uptake among older men, with mobile services proving more effective than routine facility-based services. 5. Case Study in Zimbabwe (Soccer Galas): In Masvingo Province, Zimbabwe, soccer galas were used as a platform to engage communities and deliver VMMC services. The events involved traditional, political, and religious leaders, as well as local soccer teams and schools. Services included VMMC, HIV testing, and cervical cancer screening for women. The initiative successfully circumcised 187 clients, 91% of whom were aged 15–29 years, demonstrating the effectiveness of community-driven approaches. 6. Case Study in Zimbabwe (Traditional Circumcision Integration): In Mberengwa District, Zimbabwe, the VaRemba tribe, which practices traditional male circumcision, collaborated with the Ministry of Health and Child Care (MoHCC) to integrate modern VMMC into their initiation camps. This partnership reduced adverse events and increased the uptake of medical circumcision. By 2017, 91% of circumcisions performed during the camp were medical, with minimal complications. The collaboration demonstrated respect for cultural practices while promoting safer procedures. 7. Case Study in Zimbabwe (Manicaland Province): In Manicaland Province, where traditional circumcision is not practiced, VMMC uptake among men aged 15–29 years was initially low. Barriers included limited stakeholder involvement and vertical program implementation. Interventions included engaging local leaders, improving interpersonal communication, and addressing stakeholder concerns. These efforts increased stakeholder collaboration and improved VMMC uptake. 8. Key Lessons Across Case Studies: Community involvement and ownership are critical for increasing VMMC uptake. Engaging traditional, political, and religious leaders fosters trust and collaboration. Tailored mobilization strategies, such as using soccer events or integrating services with community-based HIV testing, effectively reach target populations. Respecting cultural practices while introducing modern medical procedures can enhance acceptance and safety. Data-driven planning, including triangulating demographic and service delivery data, improves program efficiency and resource allocation. These case studies highlight the importance of innovative, culturally sensitive, and community-driven approaches to increasing VMMC uptake, ultimately contributing to HIV prevention efforts.
